acceptedAnswer.text: The math is exact for the numbers you enter. The future isn't. Returns, tax rates and interest rates change, so treat every result as an estimate to learn from, not a forecast.

json.name: Compound interest calculator
json.description: Free compound interest calculator with live sliders. See your balance grow year by year, and what starting at 22 instead of 32 is worth.

mainEntity.name: What is compound interest?

acceptedAnswer.text: It's growth on top of growth. Your money earns a return, then that return earns its own return. Over long stretches most of the final balance can come from growth, not from what you deposited.

mainEntity.name: How does this calculator do the math?

acceptedAnswer.text: It compounds monthly. Each month the balance grows by one twelfth of the yearly rate you set, then your monthly contribution is added. It repeats that for every month in the timeline.

mainEntity.name: What return should I use?

acceptedAnswer.text: That's your call, and nobody knows the future number. Try a few. A low rate, a middle one and a high one show you a range instead of a single guess. A savings account and a stock fund behave very differently, and investments can lose money.

mainEntity.name: Why does starting ten years earlier matter so much?

acceptedAnswer.text: Starting 10 years earlier adds 120 deposits. Those deposits also get more time to grow. At 0% return, the entire gap is deposits.

mainEntity.name: Does this include taxes, fees or inflation?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It's the plain math. Taxes depend on the account type, fees depend on what you hold, and inflation means future dollars buy less than today's.

json.description: Free 50/30/20 budget calculator. Enter your take-home pay, drag the sliders, and see needs, wants and savings in dollars. Download your plan.

mainEntity.name: What is the 50/30/20 budget rule?

acceptedAnswer.text: It splits take-home pay into three parts: 50% for needs, 30% for wants, and 20% for savings and extra debt payments. It's a starting point you adjust, not a rule you pass or fail.

mainEntity.name: Should I use my salary or my take-home pay?

acceptedAnswer.text: Take-home pay. That's what lands in your bank account after taxes and paycheck deductions, and it's the only money you can actually budget.

mainEntity.name: What if my needs are more than 50%?

acceptedAnswer.text: Drag the needs slider to your real number. The builder shrinks the other two to fit. A first salary or a high-rent city pushes plenty of budgets past 50%. Seeing it is step one.

mainEntity.name: What does the download include?

acceptedAnswer.text: A small CSV file with your three buckets, the percentages, and the monthly and yearly dollar amounts. It opens in Excel or Google Sheets. It's made in your browser and isn't sent anywhere.

mainEntity.name: I'm paid every two weeks. How does that work?

acceptedAnswer.text: Switch to Every 2 weeks and enter one paycheck. The builder multiplies by 26 paychecks and divides by 12 months to get your average month.

json.name: Debt payoff calculator: avalanche vs snowball
json.description: Debt payoff calculator: avalanche vs snowball, side by side. Enter your debts and see months to payoff and total interest for each method.

mainEntity.name: What is the debt avalanche method?

acceptedAnswer.text: You pay the minimum on every debt, then put all extra money toward the debt with the highest interest rate. When it's gone, you move to the next highest. It costs the least interest overall.

mainEntity.name: What is the debt snowball method?

acceptedAnswer.text: You pay the minimum on every debt, then put all extra money toward the smallest balance. When it's gone, you roll that payment into the next smallest. You get a paid-off debt sooner, and that win keeps you going.

mainEntity.name: Which one is better, avalanche or snowball?

acceptedAnswer.text: Avalanche never costs more interest than snowball. When your smallest debt isn't your highest rate, it costs less. Snowball gives quicker wins. The difference in dollars depends on your debts, which is why this calculator shows both. The plan you'll actually stick with matters more than the method.

mainEntity.name: Where do I find my APR and minimum payment?

acceptedAnswer.text: On your statement or in your lender's app. APR is the yearly interest rate. The minimum payment is the smallest amount you can pay that month without a late fee.

mainEntity.name: Are my debts saved anywhere?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only in your own browser so they're here when you come back. Nothing you enter is sent to me or to a server.

json.name: Roth vs traditional calculator
json.description: Roth vs traditional, explained first and calculated second. See how your tax rate now and later decides which one leaves you more to spend.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between Roth and traditional?

acceptedAnswer.text: It's when you pay income tax. Traditional: your contribution may lower your taxable income today, and withdrawals are taxed later. Roth: you contribute money that's already been taxed, and qualified withdrawals are tax-free.

mainEntity.name: Which is better, Roth or traditional?

acceptedAnswer.text: Neither is better across the board. Lower tax rate now than at withdrawal: Roth wins. Higher now: traditional wins. Equal rates: they tie. The catch is that nobody knows their future rate for sure.

mainEntity.name: What are the 2026 contribution limits?

acceptedAnswer.text: For 2026 the IRS limit is $7,500 for IRAs and $24,500 for 401(k) plans if you're under 50. Roth IRA contributions phase out at higher incomes: $153,000 to $168,000 for single filers and $242,000 to $252,000 for married couples filing jointly.

mainEntity.name: Can I have both a Roth and a traditional account?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Plenty of people hold both: a traditional 401(k) at work and a Roth IRA on their own. The IRA limit is shared across all your IRAs.

mainEntity.name: Is this calculator tax advice?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It uses one flat rate on each side to show the idea. Real taxes have brackets, deductions and rules that depend on your situation. A tax professional can look at your actual numbers.

mainEntity.name: What should I do with my first $1,000?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on three things: whether you have high-rate debt, whether you have any emergency cushion, and whether your job offers a retirement match. The standard order: a small buffer, high-rate debt, the match, a full emergency fund, then long-term goals.

mainEntity.name: Should I pay off debt or save first?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both, in order. Keep a $500 starter buffer so a surprise doesn't go on a card. Then put extra money at any debt charging 20% or more. After that, build the emergency fund to three to six months of expenses.

mainEntity.name: Does this quiz tell me what to invest in?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. I'm not securities licensed, and the quiz never names an investment. It covers the order of the basics and points you to the tools to run your own numbers.

mainEntity.name: Is my answer saved?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The quiz runs in your browser. If you share your result, the link only carries which plan you landed on.

mainEntity.name: Should I budget with gross pay or take-home pay?

acceptedAnswer.text: Take-home pay. It's the money you can actually spend, after taxes and paycheck deductions.

mainEntity.name: How much of my first paycheck should I save?

acceptedAnswer.text: There's no single right number. The 50/30/20 rule uses 20% of take-home pay as a target for savings and extra debt payments. If that's out of reach, start smaller and raise it when you get a raise.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a budgeting app?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A notes app or a spreadsheet works. The tool matters less than checking it once a week.

json.headline: What a Roth IRA actually is
json.description: A Roth IRA is an account, not an investment. You pay tax now so qualified withdrawals later are tax-free. 2026 limits inside.

itemListElement.name: What a Roth IRA actually is

mainEntity.name: How much can I put in a Roth IRA in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: Up to $7,500 if you're under 50, or your earned income for the year if that's less. The limit covers all your IRAs combined.

mainEntity.name: Can I take money out of a Roth IRA early?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can withdraw your contributions at any time without tax or penalty. Earnings are different. Take them out before 59 and a half, or before the account is five years old, and you can owe tax plus a 10% penalty. A few exceptions apply.

mainEntity.name: Is a Roth IRA the same as a Roth 401(k)?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A Roth 401(k) is offered through an employer and has a higher limit, $24,500 in 2026. A Roth IRA is one you open on your own. Both use after-tax money.

mainEntity.name: Do I have to pick investments?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The account only holds what you choose to put in it. Money left as cash stays cash. A licensed advisor can help with that choice, or you can research it yourself.

json.description: A credit score runs from 300 to 850. Five things move it, and two of them do most of the work. Here's the breakdown.

mainEntity.name: What is a good credit score?

acceptedAnswer.text: Lenders set their own cutoffs, so there's no single line on the 300 to 850 scale. Higher scores get better rates.

mainEntity.name: Does checking my credit score hurt it?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Checking your own score or report is a soft inquiry and has no effect. Hard inquiries come from applying for credit.

mainEntity.name: How do I start building credit with no history?

acceptedAnswer.text: Three ways in: a secured card, a student card, or being added as an authorized user on a family member's card. What matters after that is paying on time, every time.

mainEntity.name: Where can I get my credit report for free?

acceptedAnswer.text: AnnualCreditReport.com is the official site. You can get free reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion there.

mainEntity.name: How much should I have in an emergency fund?

acceptedAnswer.text: The standard target is three to six months of essential expenses. If that's far off, start with $500, then one month, and build from there.

mainEntity.name: Should I pay off debt or build an emergency fund first?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both, in order. Build a small starter fund so a surprise doesn't land on a card. Then send extra money at high-rate debt. Then finish the fund.

mainEntity.name: Where should I keep my emergency fund?

acceptedAnswer.text: In an insured savings account you can reach within a day or two, separate from your everyday checking.
